topics.title: Kamala Das and a drive to Cochin

learn.hook: A short car ride to the airport. A mother dozing in the seat beside you. In that ordinary moment, Kamala Das finds a lifetime of fear.
points: Poet: Kamala Das, an Indian poet who wrote in English and Malayalam (as Madhavikutty), known for frank, confessional poetry.
Form: a short autobiographical poem written as one long sentence, with no stanza breaks; the flow mirrors a rush of thoughts.
Situation: the poet drives from her parents' home to Cochin airport on a Friday morning.
Her mother sits beside her, dozing with her mouth open.

example.q: Why might the poet have written the poem as a single sentence?
steps: The poem records one continuous stream of thought and feeling.
A single sentence shows feelings flowing without pause.
It matches the short car ride, from home to the airport.
example.answer: The single sentence mirrors an unbroken flow of thoughts and emotions during one journey.

learn.reallife: Many Indian students living away from home in Kota, Bengaluru or Delhi know the airport goodbye with a parent. This poem captures the feeling behind it.

topics.title: A face like a corpse, a mind that turns away

learn.hook: Sometimes you notice, all at once, that a parent has grown old. The poet's first instinct is to look away.
points: Looking at her sleeping mother, the poet sees her face ashen like a corpse's and realises with pain that her mother is as old as she looks.
She pushes the thought away and looks outside at young trees sprinting past and merry children spilling out of their homes.
At the airport, after the security check, she looks at her mother again: wan and pale as a late winter's moon.
An old childhood fear returns: the fear of losing her mother, felt now as a familiar ache.

example.q: Why does the poet look out of the window?
steps: The sight of her mother's ashen face is painful.
Outside, the trees and children are full of life.
Looking away helps her escape the thought of ageing and death.
example.answer: To escape the painful thought of her mother's ageing; the lively scene outside is a distraction.

learn.reallife: Many of us scroll our phones or change the subject when a hard thought comes up. The poet's glance out of the window is the same human reflex.

topics.title: 'See you soon, Amma': love that hides its fear

learn.hook: Three simple words: 'See you soon.' Behind them lies everything the poet cannot say.
points: At parting, the poet hides her feelings and says only, 'See you soon, Amma.'
She smiles and smiles and smiles, to reassure her mother and to hide her own fear.
Theme: the ageing of a parent and the fear of separation and death.
Theme: love, helplessness and suppressed emotion; she cannot stop time, so she covers her pain with hope.

example.q: What do the parting words 'See you soon, Amma' convey?
steps: They sound casual and cheerful.
In fact they express hope that her mother will live to meet her again.
They also hide the poet's fear.
example.answer: Hope of meeting again and an attempt to hide fear and reassure her mother.

learn.reallife: Indian families often keep goodbyes light, 'Phone kar dena, beta', even when they are worried. The poet's smile is that same brave lightness.

topics.title: Youth versus age: similes and images

learn.hook: Inside the car: an old woman asleep. Outside: trees racing and children bursting out of homes. Two worlds, one window apart.
points: Theme: the contrast between youth and old age, life and decay.
Similes: the face 'ashen like that of a corpse'; the mother 'pale as a late winter's moon'.
Imagery: young trees sprinting; merry children spilling out of their homes, full of energy and joy.
Personification: the trees are described as sprinting, as if they were runners; in a moving car they seem to race past.

example.q: Why are the trees said to be 'sprinting'?
steps: From a moving car, roadside trees seem to rush backwards.
'Sprinting' gives them life and speed, like young runners.
This energy contrasts with the dozing mother.
example.answer: From the moving car they seem to run past; the word gives them youthful energy that contrasts with the mother's age.

learn.reallife: Look out of a Vande Bharat window and the trees seem to race by. The poet uses that everyday effect to say something deep about time.

topics.title: Repetition, free verse and the poet's ache

learn.hook: 'Smile and smile and smile.' Say it aloud. Does it sound happy, or does it sound like someone trying very hard?
points: Repetition: 'smile and smile and smile' shows the effort of keeping up a brave face; the smile hides pain.
Structure: the contrast between inside the car (age) and outside (youth); enjambment, with lines running on; free verse, with no regular rhyme or metre.
The poet's pain is the realisation that her mother is old and may soon die; the ache is her childhood fear of losing her mother, now returning.
The trees are 'sprinting' because, from a moving car, they appear to rush backwards, and they stand for youth hurrying past.

example.q: What kind of pain and ache does the poet feel?
steps: Pain: realising her mother is truly old.
Ache: an old childhood fear of losing her.
Both come from love and the fear of separation by death.
example.answer: The pain of seeing her mother's age and the ache of her old fear of losing her for ever.

learn.reallife: Indian film songs often repeat a line to show feeling. Kamala Das's triple smile works the same way: the repetition is the emotion.

topics.title: Board exam practice: My Mother at Sixty-six

learn.hook: Extract-based questions on this poem almost always ask about a simile or the contrast. Let's practise.
points: Merry children: brought in to contrast youth and joy with the mother's old age and to distract the poet from her pain.
Late winter's moon: like the moon at the end of winter, the mother is pale, dim and near the end of her life.
Parting words and smile: hope of meeting again, and a brave mask over her fear.
Extract-based MCQs: identify similes ('ashen like', 'pale as'), the contrast between inside and outside, the poet's feelings; short answers on her fear.

example.q: Extract (paraphrased): after security, she looks at her mother again, pale like a late winter's moon, and feels the old ache. (a) Device? (b) Feeling?
steps: 'Pale as a late winter's moon' uses 'as': a simile.
The 'old familiar ache' is her childhood fear.
Feeling: fear of losing her mother.
example.answer: (a) Simile. (b) Fear and pain at the thought of losing her mother.

learn.reallife: CBSE extract questions reward precise terms. Writing 'simile' with the exact words, rather than 'comparison', can earn the full mark.
